comment: The paired protocols of K6, from one source. Every benchmark here is run
on two backends -- this kernel, and Linux on the same virtual machine --
from the same C source, with only the primitive under measurement
differing, and this file is where both sides and their judge read what a
benchmark is, what each side does for it, and what the comparison is
allowed to conclude. `tools/gen_k6_bench.py` derives the C header both C
builds include and the Rust module the native supervisor reads;
`tools/check_k6_bench.py` regenerates and compares.
`equivalence` is the part that decides what a result may say, and it is
decided here, before anything is measured:
equivalent   the same contract on both sides. A difference whose
confidence interval excludes no-difference may be stated as
a speed difference of that primitive on this platform.
comparable   the same question answered by primitives with different
guarantees, listed in `differences`. The two costs are
reported side by side with their ratio; the conclusion is
about each primitive with its guarantees, never that one
kernel is faster.
different    the two sides do different things that answer related
questions. Both numbers are reported; no ratio is
interpreted.
native_only  a characterization of a mechanism Linux does not have in
this form. No comparison.
Samples are time-stamp-counter cycles unless `unit` says otherwise. Both
backends read the same counter on the same virtual machine, and each
calibrates it against its own monotonic clock and reports the result, so
a disagreement between the two calibrations is visible rather than hidden
inside a conversion.
The ROLE_, SLOT_, _BIT and SHARED_ constants are the agreement between the
native supervisor and the native benchmark program: which role a domain is
built as, which capability slot holds which facet, which signal bits hand
an entry from the program to the supervisor and back, and where the plan
and a handoff request sit in the page the supervisor shares with the
program. The Linux build ignores them; they name nothing there.

PLAN.doc: The plan this run follows. Value: its seed.

TSC_HZ.doc: Time-stamp-counter frequency calibrated against this backend's monotonic clock over CAL_WINDOW_NS.

BEGIN.doc: A benchmark starts. Value: id | param << 16 | samples << 32.

SAMPLE.doc: Two samples, the earlier in the low 32 bits. LOST_SAMPLE marks a sample that was not taken.

END.doc: A benchmark ended. Value: id | errors << 32.

ERROR.doc: An operation under measurement failed. Value: id | (status & 0xffffffff) << 32.

MISMATCH.doc: An engine answer was not the reference completion. Value: prompt index.

CHECK.doc: A correctness check the benchmark makes on its own work passed. Value: id | count << 32.

AUX.doc: A benchmark-specific quantity. Value: id | quantity index << 16 | value << 32.

DONE.doc: The plan ran to its end. Value: benchmarks run.

DIGEST.doc: FNV-1a of the first answer an engine gave to one prompt. Value: the digest; the prompt is the AUX note before it.

families.primitive: What one kernel primitive costs, with its guarantees described (linux-comparison question 1).
families.sched: Scheduling behaviour a program observes: how long a woken thread waits to run.
families.quota: How closely an aggregate CPU budget is enforced.
families.scale: Throughput as independent work is added on four processors.
families.closure: Stopping a unit of work and getting its resources back.
families.engine: The real load: Thalyx's resident engine answering the fixture's questions (linux-comparison question 2).
families.v0: Data for re-evaluating the V0 interface parameters.

benchmarks.name: entry.version
benchmarks.native: the VERSION_QUERY entry: no descriptor, no object, no lock

benchmarks.name: entry.clock
benchmarks.native: the CLOCK_QUERY entry: a monotonic reading converted in the kernel

benchmarks.name: ipc.call
benchmarks.native: ENDPOINT_CALL from one domain to another that answers with RECEIVE and INVOCATION_REPLY, the payload copied both ways
benchmarks.linux: a SOCK_SEQPACKET socket pair between two processes: send and recv, the server receiving with SO_PASSCRED so every message carries the sender's credentials, the payload copied both ways
differences: native: the kernel stamps origin domain, origin scope, facet and causal parent into a header the payload cannot overwrite; linux: the kernel attaches pid, uid and gid
native: every admission reserves and writes a control receipt, which an auditor has to drain; linux: nothing is recorded
native: queue bytes are charged to the caller's scope and an invocation object is created and discharged; linux: socket buffer accounting against the sender
native: the reply is a one-shot object bound to the invocation; linux: any later message on the socket

benchmarks.name: ipc.caps
benchmarks.native: ENDPOINT_CALL copying N capabilities to memory objects into the receiver, which closes them before replying
benchmarks.linux: sendmsg with SCM_RIGHTS carrying N descriptors of memfd objects; the receiver closes them before replying
differences: native: every capability is a grant in the caller's lineage, installed in the receiver at admission, all or none, and charged as metadata; linux: descriptors are duplicated into the receiver's table at receive
native: the batch is refused whole if the receiver has no room; linux: descriptors that do not fit are discarded with MSG_CTRUNC

benchmarks.name: mem.map
benchmarks.native: SCOPE_CREATE_MEMORY, DOMAIN_MAP, a write to every page, DOMAIN_UNMAP and CAP_CLOSE
benchmarks.linux: mmap of anonymous private memory, a write to every page, munmap
differences: native: pages are zeroed and charged to the caller's scope when the object is created; linux: pages are allocated and zeroed on first touch and charged to the process
native: DOMAIN_UNMAP does not return until every processor the domain ran on has acknowledged the invalidation; linux: munmap invalidates the processors in the mm's cpumask

benchmarks.name: mem.seal
benchmarks.native: create an object, map it writable, write it, MEMORY_SEAL (which withdraws the writable mapping and waits for every processor), map it read-only, read it, unmap, close
benchmarks.linux: memfd_create, ftruncate, mmap writable, write, munmap, F_ADD_SEALS with F_SEAL_WRITE|F_SEAL_SHRINK|F_SEAL_GROW, mmap read-only, read, munmap, close
differences: native: the seal withdraws writable mappings itself; linux: sealing is refused while a writable mapping exists, so the program removes it first
native: after the seal no writer exists in the declared perimeter, DMA excepted under the weak profile; linux: the same for the file's mappings

benchmarks.name: cap.derive
benchmarks.native: CAP_DERIVE narrowing the rights of a memory capability, then CAP_CLOSE of the derived handle
benchmarks.linux: fcntl(F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC) of a memfd descriptor, then close
differences: native: the derived grant narrows rights, joins the lineage a barrier reaches, and is charged as metadata; linux: the duplicate carries the same rights and nothing can close the lineage

benchmarks.name: sched.wake
benchmarks.native: a thread raises a signal another thread of the same domain is blocked on and keeps running; the sample is the time until the woken thread executes
benchmarks.linux: a thread wakes another thread of the same process blocked in FUTEX_WAIT and keeps running; the sample is the time until the woken thread executes

benchmarks.name: quota.share
benchmarks.native: a thread that never blocks, in a scope whose budget is the given share of each 10 ms window; the sample is the execution it received in one window
benchmarks.linux: a thread that never blocks, in a cgroup whose cpu.max is the given share of a 10 ms period; the sample is the execution it received in one period

benchmarks.name: scale.ipc
benchmarks.native: N independent caller/answerer pairs on N endpoints; the sample is round trips completed by all pairs in one 10 ms slice
benchmarks.linux: N independent SOCK_SEQPACKET pairs; the sample is round trips completed by all pairs in one 10 ms slice
differences: native: the guarantees of ipc.call, including a receipt per admission that one auditor drains for all pairs
native: one machine lock serialises every kernel entry that touches an object; linux: per-socket locks

benchmarks.name: scale.compute
benchmarks.native: N threads running a fixed integer loop with no kernel entry; the sample is loop iterations completed by all threads in one 10 ms slice
benchmarks.linux: the same loop in N threads of one process

benchmarks.name: closure.unit
benchmarks.native: SCOPE_FENCE, DOMAIN_TERMINATE and SCOPE_RETIRE, until the retirement succeeds, of a scope whose one domain has signalled that it is about to block in the kernel; quantities 1-4 break the first sample into fence, terminate and retire microseconds and retire attempts
benchmarks.linux: SIGKILL to a child process blocked in the kernel, then waitpid
differences: native: the barrier also reaches every capability derived under the scope, withdraws its undelivered messages, and the retirement is refused until nothing it sponsors is outstanding; linux: the process ends and its descriptors close
native: the domain's frames pass through a quarantine that waits for every processor's invalidation before reuse; linux: pages are freed as the mm is torn down

benchmarks.name: engine.load
benchmarks.native: from activating the engine domain to its ready signal: llama.cpp loads the pinned model from the sealed object into memory charged to the engine's scope
benchmarks.linux: from fork of Thalyx's engine, unchanged, to its ready frame: llama.cpp loads the same model with mmap
differences: native: the weights are read into memory the engine's scope pays for; linux: the model file is mapped
native: the libc, allocator and math library are this repository's; linux: glibc

benchmarks.name: engine.infer
benchmarks.native: one request to the resident engine with the fixture's prompt, answered with the same completion the reference gives; the sample is the caller's time from request to answer
benchmarks.linux: one request frame to Thalyx's engine, unchanged, with the same prompt; the sample is the caller's time from request to answer
differences: the libc, allocator and math library differ, and the answer is checked byte for byte against the reference so the work is the same work

benchmarks.name: engine.cancel
benchmarks.native: a request for a long answer is cancelled by fencing the caller's scope; the sample is the time from the fence to the next answered request from another caller, the engine staying resident
benchmarks.linux: a request for a long answer is cancelled by SIGKILL to the engine, as the Linux profile declares; the sample is the time from the signal to the next answered request, which needs the engine started and loaded again
differences: this is the declared cancellation mechanism of each profile, not the same mechanism: scope_closure_between_tokens against process_signal

benchmarks.name: ipc.lineage
benchmarks.native: ENDPOINT_CALL with no payload through a facet the caller derived further by the given number of steps, so admission walks that many more grants; the facet's own depth is reported beside it

benchmarks.name: audit.drain
benchmarks.native: LOG_READ and LOG_ACK of one batch of receipts by the auditor, per batch of RECEIPT_BATCH

structs.name: Plan
structs.doc: What one boot runs, in order. The same bytes reach both backends: a module of the native package, a file of the Linux one.

fields.name: seed
fields.doc: Seed the host drew for this boot; it decided the order of the entries.

fields.name: round
fields.doc: Which round of the paired design this boot is.

fields.name: model_bytes
fields.doc: Bytes of the engine model the package carries; a sealed module is whole pages, so the length is said here and checked against the object. Zero when no entry asks the engine. Linux reads the file and ignores it.

fields.name: bench
fields.doc: Benchmark ids, in the order they run.

structs.name: Handoff
structs.doc: An entry the native program hands to its supervisor, which runs it and answers with HANDOFF_DONE_BIT. At SHARED_HANDOFF_OFFSET.

fields.name: status
fields.doc: Written by the supervisor: zero, or the negated status it stopped with.
